section.paragraph: the exponential function is, without doubt, the most important function in mathematics and its applications. After a brief introduction to the exponential function and its inverse, the logarithmic function, we learn how to differentiate such functions. This lays the foundation for exploring the many applications involving exponential functions. For example, we look at the role played by exponential functions in computing earned interest on a bank account and in studying the growth of a bacteria population in the laboratory, the rate at which radioactive matter decays, the rate at which a factory worker learns a certain process, and the rate at which a communicable disease is spread over time.

section.paragraph: Exponential functions play an important role in mathematical analysis. Because of their special characteristics, they are some of the most useful functions and are found in virtually every field in which mathematics is applied. To mention a few examples: Under ideal conditions, the number of bacteria present at any time $$t$$ in a culture may be described by an exponential function of $$t$$ ; radioactive substances decay over time in accordance with an “exponential” law of decay; money left on fixed deposit and earning compound interest grows exponentially; and some of the most important distribution functions encountered in statistics are exponential.
Let’s begin our investigation into the properties of exponential functions by studying their graphs.

note.title: Properties of the Exponential Function
note.heading: Properties of the Exponential Function
note.paragraph: The exponential function $$y = b^{x}\left( {b > 0,b \neq 1} \right)$$ has the following properties:

list.item: Its domain is $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ .
Its range is $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ .
Its graph passes through the point $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ .
It is continuous on $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ .
It is increasing on $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ if $$b > 1$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ if $$b < 1$$ .

section.heading: 5.2. Logarithmic Functions
Logarithms
section.paragraph: You are already familiar with exponential equations of the form
$${b^{y} = x} \left( {b > 0,b \neq 1} \right)$$

where the variable $$x$$ is expressed in terms of a real number $$b$$ and a variable $$y$$ . But what about solving this same equation for $$y$$ ? You may recall from your study of algebra that the number $$y$$ is called the logarithm of $$\mathbf{x}$$ to the base $$\mathbf{b}$$ and is denoted by $$\mathbf{\log_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{x}}$$ . It is the power to which the base $$b$$ must be raised to obtain the number $$x$$ .

section.paragraph: The two most widely used systems of logarithms are the system of common logarithms , which uses the number $$10$$ as its base, and the system of natural logarithms , which uses the irrational number $$e = 2.71828\ldots$$ as its base. section.paragraph: The definition of a logarithm implies that if $$b$$ and $$n$$ are positive numbers and $$b$$ is different from $$1$$ , then the expression $$\log_{b}n$$ is a real number. This enables us to define a logarithmic function as follows.

note.paragraph: The function defined by
$$f(x) = \log_{b}x \left( {b > 0,b \neq 1} \right)$$
is called the logarithmic function with base $$\mathbf{b}$$ . The domain of $$f$$ is the set of all positive numbers.

section.paragraph: One easy way to obtain the graph of the logarithmic function $$y = \log_{b}x$$ is to construct a table of values of the logarithm (base $$b$$ ). If a point $$(u,v)$$ lies on the graph of $$y = \log_{b}x$$ , then

note.paragraph: The logarithmic function $${y = \log_{b}x}\left( {b > 0,b \neq 1} \right)$$ has the following properties:

It is increasing on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ if $$b > 1$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ if $$b < 1$$ .

section.paragraph: We made use of the relationship that exists between the exponential function $$f(x) = e^{x}$$ and the logarithmic function $$g(x) = \ln x$$ when we sketched the graph of $$g$$ in Example 6. This relationship is further described by the following properties, which are an immediate consequence of the definition of the logarithm of a number.

From Properties 2 and 3, we conclude that the composite function satisfies

$$\begin{array}{rcll} {\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x)} & = & {f\left\lbrack {g(x)} \right\rbrack} & \\ & = & {e^{\ln x} = x} & \left( { \text{for all} x > 0} \right) \\ {\left( {g \circ f} \right)(x)} & = & {g\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack} & \\ & = & {\ln e^{x} = x} & \left( { \text{for all} x > 0} \right) \end{array}$$

Any two functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ that satisfy this relationship are said to be inverses of each other. Note that the function $$f$$ undoes what the function $$g$$ does, and vice versa, so the composition of the two functions in any order results in the identity function $$F(x) = x$$ .*

section.heading: 5.3. Compound Interest
Compound Interest
section.paragraph: Compound interest is a natural application of the exponential function to the business world. We begin by recalling that simple interest is interest that is computed only on the original principal. Thus, if $$I$$ denotes the interest on a principal $$P$$ (in dollars) at an interest rate of $$r$$ per year for $$t$$ years, then we have
$$I = Prt$$
The accumulated amount $$A$$ , the sum of the principal and interest after $$t$$ years, is given by
$$\begin{array}{l} {A{= P + I = P +}{Prt}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= P\left( {1 + rt} \right)} \text{Simple interest formula} } \end{array}$$

Frequently, interest earned is periodically added to the principal and thereafter earns interest itself at the same rate. This is called compound interest . To find a formula for the accumulated amount, let’s consider a numerical example. Suppose $$\$ 1000$$ (the principal) is deposited in a bank for a term of $$3$$ years, earning interest at the rate of $$8\%$$ per year (called the nominal, or stated, rate) compounded annually. Then, using Formula (4) with $$P = 1000$$ , $$r = 0.08$$ , and $$t = 1$$ , we see that the accumulated amount at the end of the first year is
$$\begin{array}{l} {A_{1}{= P\left( {1 + rt} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{A_{1}}{= 1000\left\lbrack {1 + 0.08(1)} \right\rbrack}{= 1000(1.08) = 1080}} \end{array}$$

To find the accumulated amount $$A_{2}$$ at the end of the second year, we use Equation (4) once again, this time with $$P = A_{1}$$ . (Remember, the principal and interest now earn interest over the second year.) We obtain

$$\begin{array}{l} {A_{2} = {P\left( {1 + rt} \right) = A_{1}\left( {1 + rt} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{A_{2}} = {1000\left\lbrack {1 + 0.08(1)} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack {1 + 0.08(1)} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{A_{2}} = {1000\left( {1 + 0.08} \right)^{2} = 1000(1.08)^{2} = 1166.40}} \end{array}$$
Finally, the accumulated amount $$A_{3}$$ at the end of the third year is found by using Equation (4) with $$P = A_{2}$$ , giving

$$\begin{array}{l} {A_{3} = {P\left( {1 + rt} \right) = A_{2}\left( {1 + rt} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{A_{3}} = {1000\left\lbrack {1 + 0.08(1)} \right\rbrack^{2}\left\lbrack {1 + 0.08(1)} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{A_{3}} = {1000\left( {1 + 0.08} \right)^{3} = 1000(1.08)^{3} \approx 1259.71}} \end{array}$$
or approximately $$\$ 1259.71$$ .

These observations suggest the following general result: If $$P$$ dollars are invested over a term of $$t$$ years earning interest at the rate of $$r$$ per year compounded annually, then the accumulated amount is
$$A = P\left( {1 + r} \right)^{t}$$

Formula (5) was derived under the assumption that interest was compounded annually. In practice, however, interest is usually compounded more than once a year. The interval of time between successive interest calculations is called the conversion period.
If interest at a nominal rate of $$r$$ per year is compounded $$m$$ times a year on a principal of $$P$$ dollars, then the simple interest rate per conversion period is
$${i = \frac{r}{m}} \frac{ \text{Annual interest rate} }{ \text{Periods per year} }$$

section.heading: Effective Rate of Interest
section.paragraph: In Example 1, we saw that the interest earned on an investment depends on the frequency with which the interest is compounded. Thus, the stated, or nominal, rate of $$8\%$$ per year does not reflect the actual rate at which interest is earned. This suggests that we need to find a common basis for comparing interest rates. One way of comparing interest rates is provided by using the effective rate. The effective rate is the simple interest rate that would produce the same accumulated amount in $$1$$ year as the nominal rate compounded $$m$$ times a year. The effective rate is also called the true rate.

To derive a relation between the nominal interest rate, $$r$$ per year compounded $$m$$ times and its corresponding effective rate, $$r_{eff}$$ per year, let’s assume an initial investment of $$P$$ dollars. Then, the accumulated amount after $$1$$ year at a simple interest rate of $$r_{eff}$$ per year is
$$A = P\left( {1 + r_{eff}} \right)$$
Also, the accumulated amount after $$1$$ year at an interest rate of $$r$$ per year compounded $$m$$ times a year is
$$A {= P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{m}} \right)^{m}} {{Since}t = 1}$$
Equating the two expressions gives

$$\begin{array}{rcl} {P\left( {1 + r_{eff}} \right)} & = & {P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{m}} \right)^{m}} \\ {1 + r_{eff}} & = & {\left( {1 + \frac{r}{m}} \right)^{m} { \text{Divide both sides by} P.}} \end{array}$$
or, upon solving for $$r_{eff}$$ , we obtain the formula for computing the effective rate of interest:

note.title: Effective Rate of Interest Formula
note.heading: Effective Rate of Interest Formula
note.paragraph: $$r_{eff} = \left( {1 + \frac{r}{m}} \right)^{m} - 1$$
where
$$\begin{array}{rcl} r_{eff} & = & \text{Effective rate of interest} \\ r & = & \text{Nominal interest rate per year} \\ m & = & \text{Number of conversion periods per year} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Now, if the effective rate of interest $$r_{eff}$$ is known, then the accumulated amount after $$t$$ years on an investment of $$P$$ dollars may be more readily computed by using the formula
$$A = P\left( {1 + r_{eff}} \right)^{t}$$

The 1968 Truth in Lending Act passed by Congress requires that the effective rate of interest be disclosed in all contracts involving interest charges. The passage of this act has benefited consumers because they now have a common basis for comparing the various nominal rates quoted by different financial institutions. Furthermore, knowing the effective rate enables consumers to compute the actual charges involved in a transaction. The effective rate is also called the annual percentage yield (APY). section.paragraph: One question that arises naturally in the study of compound interest is: What happens to the accumulated amount over a fixed period of time if the interest is computed more and more frequently?

Intuition suggests that the more often interest is compounded, the larger the accumulated amount will be. This is confirmed by the results of Example 1, in which we found that the accumulated amounts did in fact increase when we increased the number of conversion periods per year.

section.heading: Logarithmic Differentiation
section.paragraph: As we saw in Examples 3 and 4, the task of finding the derivative of a given function can sometimes be made easier by first applying the laws of logarithms to simplify the function. We now illustrate a process called logarithmic differentiation , which not only simplifies the calculation of the derivatives of certain functions but also enables us to compute the derivatives of functions that we could not otherwise differentiate using the techniques developed thus far.

note.heading: Applied Example 1. Growth of Bacteria
note.paragraph: Under ideal laboratory conditions, the number of bacteria in a culture grows in accordance with the law $$Q(t) = Q_{0}e^{\mathit{kt}}$$ , where $$Q_{0}$$ denotes the number of bacteria initially present in the culture, $$k$$ is a constant determined by the strain of bacteria under consideration and other factors, and $$t$$ is the elapsed time measured in hours. Suppose $$10,000$$ bacteria are present initially in the culture and $$60,000$$ present $$2$$ hours later.

list.item: How many bacteria will there be in the culture at the end of $$4$$ hours?
What is the rate of growth of the population after $$4$$ hours?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: We are given that $$Q(0) = Q_{0} = 10,000$$ , so $$Q(t) = 10,000e^{\mathit{kt}}$$ . Next, the fact that $$60,000$$ bacteria are present $$2$$ hours later translates into $$Q(2) = 60,000$$ . Thus, $$\begin{array}{ccl} 60,000 & = & {10,000e^{2k}} \\ e^{2k} & = & 6 \end{array}$$ Taking the natural logarithm on both sides of the equation, we obtain $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\ln e^{2k}} & = & {\ln 6} \\ {2k} & = & {{\ln 6} { \text{Since} \ln e = 1}} \\ k & = & \frac{\ln 6}{2} \\ k & \approx & 0.8959 \end{array}$$ Thus, the number of bacteria present at any time $$t$$ is given by $$Q(t) \approx 10,000e^{0.8959t}$$ In particular, the number of bacteria present in the culture at the end of $$4$$ hours is given by $$\begin{array}{lll} {Q(4)} & \approx & {10,000e^{0.8959{(4)}}} \\ & \approx & 360,000 \end{array}$$

The rate of growth of the bacteria population at any time $$t$$ is given by $$Q^{\prime}(t) = kQ(t)$$ Thus, using the result from part (a), we find that the rate at which the population is growing at the end of $$4$$ hours is $$\begin{array}{l} {{Q^{\prime}(4)} = {kQ(4)}} \\ {\phantom{Q^{\prime}(4)} \approx {(0.8959)(360,000)}} \\ {\phantom{Q^{\prime}(4)} \approx 322,500} \end{array}$$ or approximately $$322,500$$ bacteria per hour.

Historically, the world’s oceans were thought to provide an unlimited source of inexpensive seafood. However, in a world in which the human population now exceeds six billion people, overfishing has pushed one third of all marine fishery stocks toward a state of collapse.

As a fishery geneticist at Hopkins Marine Station, I study commercially harvested marine populations and use exponential models in my work. The equation for determining the size of a population that grows or declines exponentially is $$x_{t} = x_{0}e^{\mathit{rt}}$$ , where $$x_{0}$$ is the initial population, $$t$$ is time, and $$r$$ is the growth or decay constant (positive for growth, negative for decay).

This equation can be used to estimate the population in the past as well as in the future. We know that the demand for seafood increased as the human population grew, eventually causing fish populations to decline. Because genetic diversity is linked to population size, the exponential function is useful to model change in fishery populations and their gene pools over time.

Interestingly, exponential functions can also be used to model the increase in the market value of seafood in the United States over the past $$60$$ years. In general, the price of seafood has increased exponentially, although the price did stabilize briefly in 1995.

Although exponential curves are important to my work, they are not always the best fit. Exponential curves are best applied across short time frames when environments or markets are unlimited. Over longer periods, the logistic growth function is more suitable. In my research, selecting the most accurate model requires examining many possibilities.

Next, the datum concerning the half-life of radium implies that $$Q(1600) = 100$$ , and this gives $$\begin{array}{rcl} 100 & = & {200e^{- 1600k}} \\ e^{- 1600k} & = & \frac{1}{2} \end{array}$$ Taking the natural logarithm on both sides of this equation yields $$\begin{array}{rcl} {- 1600k\ln e} & = & {\ln\frac{1}{2}} \\ {- 1600k} & = & {{\ln\frac{1}{2}} {\ln e = 1}} \\ k & = & {- \frac{1}{1600}\ln\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \approx 0.0004332} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the amount of radium left after $$t$$ years is $$Q(t) = 200e^{- 0.0004332t}$$

list.item: The given information implies that $$Q(7) = \frac{5000}{1 + 1249e^{- 7k}} = 40$$ Thus, $$\begin{array}{rcl} {40\left( {1 + 1249e^{- 7k}} \right)} & = & 5000 \\ {1 + 1249e^{- 7k}} & = & {\frac{5000}{40} = 125} \\ e^{- 7k} & = & \frac{124}{1249} \\ {- 7k} & = & {\ln\frac{124}{1249}} \\ k & = & {- \frac{\ln\frac{124}{1249}}{7} \approx 0.33} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the number of soldiers who contracted the flu after $$t$$ days is given by $$Q(t) = \frac{5000}{1 + 1249e^{- 0.33t}}$$ In particular, the number of soldiers who contracted the flu by day $$15$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{Q(15)} = \frac{5000}{1 + 1249e^{- 15{(0.33)}}}} \\ {\phantom{Q(15)} \approx 508} \end{array}$$ or approximately $$508$$ soldiers.

The rate at which the number of soldiers contracting the flu on day $$t$$ is changing is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{Q^{\prime}(t)} = {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack \frac{5000}{1 + 1249e^{- 0.33t}} \right\rbrack = 5000\frac{d}{dt}{\lbrack{(1 + 1249e^{- 0.33t})}^{- 1}\rbrack}}} \\ {\phantom{Q^{\prime}(t)} = {(5000)( - 1){(1 + 1249e^{- 0.33t})}^{- 2} \cdot \frac{d}{dt}{({1 + 1249e^{- 0.33t}})}}} \\ {\phantom{Q^{\prime}(t)} = \frac{( - 5000)(1249)( - 0.33)e^{- 0.33t}}{{(1 + 1249e^{- 0.33t})}^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{Q^{\prime}(t)} = \frac{2,060,850e^{- 0.33t}}{{(1 + 1249e^{- 0.33t})}^{2}}} \end{array}$$ So the rate at which the number of soldiers contracting the flu is changing on day $$15$$ is $$Q^{\prime}(15) = \frac{2,060,850e^{( - 0.33)(15)}}{{(1 + 1249e^{( - 0.33)(15)})}^{2}} \approx 150.54$$ or approximately $$151$$ soldiers per day.

In the compound interest formula $$A = P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{m}} \right)^{\mathit{mt}}$$ , $$A$$ stands for the accumulated amount, $$P$$ stands for the principal, $$r$$ stands for the nominal interest rate per year, $$m$$ stands for the number of conversion periods per year, and $$t$$ stands for the term.
The effective rate $$r_{eff}$$ is related to the nominal interest rate $$r$$ per year and the number of conversion periods per year by $$r_{eff} =$$ $$\left( {1 + \frac{r}{m}} \right)^{m} - 1$$ .
If interest earned at the rate of $$r$$ per year is compounded continuously over $$t$$ years, then a principal of $$P$$ dollars will have an accumulated value of $$A =$$ $$Pe^{\mathit{rt}}$$ dollars.

If $$g(x) = e^{f{(x)}}$$ , where $$f$$ is a differentiable function, then $$g^{\prime}(x) =$$ $$e^{f{(x)}}f^{\prime}{(x)}$$ . If $$g(x) = \ln f{(x)}$$ , where $$f{(x)} > 0$$ is differentiable, then $$g^{\prime}(x) =$$ $$\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}$$ .

In the unrestricted exponential growth model $$Q = Q_{0}e^{\mathit{kt}}$$ , $$Q_{0}$$ represents the quantity present initially, and $$k$$ is called the growth constant. In the exponential decay model $$Q = Q_{0}e^{- kt}$$ , $$k$$ is called the decay constant. The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time required for a substance to decay to one half of its original amount.

For the model $$Q(t) = C - Ae^{- kt}$$ describing a learning curve, $$y = C$$ is a/an horizontal asymptote of the graph of $$Q$$ . The value of $$Q(t)$$ never exceeds $$C$$ . For the logistic growth model $$Q(t) = \frac{A}{1 + Be^{- kt}}$$ , $$y = A$$ is a/an horizontal asymptote of the graph of $$Q$$ . If the quantity $$Q(t)$$ is initially smaller than $$A$$ , then $$Q(t)$$ will eventually approach $$A$$ as $$t$$ increases; the number $$A$$ represents the life-support capacity of the environment and is called the carrying capacity of the environment.
